A process is a running program with its own operating-system resources. A thread is a worker inside that process. These ideas are related, but they are not interchangeable.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Modern .NET and older textbook terminology

  • System.Diagnostics.Process inspects processes and can start other programs. Dispose Process objects you create. Do not start arbitrary commands from untrusted input.
  • The CLR runs managed code and manages type safety, exceptions and garbage collection. AppDomain.CurrentDomain is still available for information. Creating and unloading secondary AppDomains is a .NET Framework technique, not a modern .NET isolation recipe.
  • Modern .NET uses AssemblyLoadContext for loading assemblies. A collectible context can support unloadable plugins but is not a security sandbox.
  • Object contexts in older .NET Framework remoting describe groups of context-bound objects with shared services. ContextBoundObject and remoting are legacy subjects. In ASP.NET Core, an HTTP context and an EF DbContext are different concepts.

Try it

using var process = Process.GetCurrentProcess();
Console.WriteLine(process.ProcessName);
Console.WriteLine(AppDomain.CurrentDomain.FriendlyName);

Expected output includes the executable or host name. It varies by machine and launch method. Do not memorise a fixed process ID.

Try it yourself

Is an EF DbContext a separate process?

Worked answer

No. It is an object that tracks database work inside your application process.

What should isolate an untrusted plugin?

Worked answer

A separately secured process or container boundary, with carefully controlled permissions. AssemblyLoadContext alone is not a security boundary.
